lessonTitle: The Pentose Phosphate Pathway: NADPH and Ribose Supply

blocks.text: Two days after a family feast of broad (fava) beans, a 6-year-old boy has dark urine, pale skin and yellow eyes. His red cells are being destroyed in the blood. The beans contain compounds that generate oxidants, and the boy's red cells cannot cope. The reason lies in a side route of glucose metabolism that makes no ATP at all, but supplies the reducing power that protects every red cell.

blocks.markdown: **The idea.** Besides glycolysis, glucose-6-phosphate can enter the **pentose phosphate pathway (PPP)**, a cytosolic route with two jobs: it makes **NADPH** (the reducing agent for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence) and **ribose-5-phosphate** (the sugar of nucleotides). The pathway does not produce or consume ATP. It is most active in tissues that make fatty acids or steroids (liver, adipose tissue, adrenal cortex, gonads, lactating mammary gland) and in red cells, which need NADPH for protection. Skeletal muscle has little activity.

blocks.title: NADPH versus NADH
blocks.text: NADPH is the phosphorylated form of NADH. NADH feeds the respiratory chain to make ATP (cell ratio NAD+/NADH is high, favouring oxidation). NADPH feeds reductive reactions (cell ratio NADPH/NADP+ is high, favouring reduction). They are kept in separate pools and are not interchangeable.

blocks.markdown: **Oxidative phase (irreversible, makes NADPH).** (1) **Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)** oxidises glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-lactone, reducing NADP+ to NADPH. This is the **rate-limiting and regulated** step, strongly inhibited by NADPH and stimulated by NADP+, so the pathway runs faster only when NADPH is being consumed. (2) The lactone is hydrolysed to 6-phosphogluconate. (3) **6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase** oxidatively decarboxylates it to ribulose-5-phosphate, CO2 and a second NADPH. Each glucose-6-phosphate entering the oxidative phase therefore yields **2 NADPH and 1 CO2**.

blocks.caption: Net equation of the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway.

blocks.markdown: **Non-oxidative phase (reversible, rearranges sugars).** Ribulose-5-phosphate is isomerised to **ribose-5-phosphate** or epimerised to xylulose-5-phosphate. **Transketolase** (which needs thiamine pyrophosphate) and **transaldolase** then shuffle carbon units among 3-, 4-, 5-, 6- and 7-carbon sugars, producing fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate that rejoin glycolysis. Because the phase is reversible, the cell can adapt: when NADPH is needed but not ribose, excess pentoses are recycled to glycolytic intermediates; when ribose is needed (dividing cells) but not NADPH, ribose-5-phosphate can be made from glycolytic intermediates by running the phase backwards.

rows: Oxidative phase runs; pentoses are recycled to fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
Non-oxidative phase runs backwards from glycolytic intermediates
Oxidative phase yields NADPH and ribulose-5-phosphate, which gives ribose-5-phosphate
Oxidative phase driven by NADP+ supply
blocks.caption: The pentose phosphate pathway adjusts to the cell's needs.

blocks.markdown: **Uses of NADPH.** (1) **Reductive biosynthesis**: fatty acid synthesis (14 NADPH per palmitate formed from acetyl-CoA), cholesterol and steroid hormone synthesis. (2) **Antioxidant defence**: glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH) from oxidised glutathione (GSSG). GSH is consumed by glutathione peroxidase when it reduces hydrogen peroxide to water: 2 GSH + H2O2 gives GSSG + 2 H2O; then GSSG + NADPH gives 2 GSH + NADP+. (3) **Cytochrome P450** hydroxylation of drugs and steroids. (4) The **respiratory burst** of phagocytes, in which NADPH oxidase produces superoxide to kill bacteria (defective in chronic granulomatous disease, leading to recurrent infections), and nitric oxide synthesis.

blocks.title: NADPH for fatty acid synthesis
blocks.prompt: Making one molecule of palmitate from acetyl-CoA needs 14 NADPH. If all NADPH came from the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, how many molecules of glucose-6-phosphate would be needed for one palmitate?

steps.text: Each glucose-6-phosphate passing through the oxidative phase gives 2 NADPH.
The 7 CO2 released show that the carbon is lost while the reducing power is retained.

blocks.answer: 7 glucose-6-phosphate per palmitate. In reality other sources (such as malic enzyme) also contribute.

blocks.markdown: **G6PD deficiency.** This is the commonest human enzyme deficiency, an **X-linked recessive** condition (so mostly males, and some heterozygous females). Most affected people are well until an **oxidant stress**: fava beans, certain drugs (for example primaquine, dapsone, some sulfonamides) or infection. Oxidants generate hydrogen peroxide, which glutathione peroxidase can only remove if GSH is available. Without enough NADPH, glutathione reductase cannot regenerate GSH, haemoglobin is oxidised and precipitates as **Heinz bodies**, membranes are damaged, and the spleen removes the damaged cells (**bite cells**), giving **acute haemolytic anaemia** with jaundice and dark urine. Red cells are especially vulnerable because the PPP is their **only source of NADPH** (they lack mitochondria and cannot make new enzyme). The condition is common in regions where malaria was endemic, since it confers some protection.

blocks.title: NADPH cost of detoxifying hydrogen peroxide
blocks.prompt: A red cell exposed to an oxidant forms 4 micromol of hydrogen peroxide. How many micromol of glucose-6-phosphate must be oxidised in the PPP to restore the glutathione used?

steps.text: Each H2O2 consumes 2 GSH, so 4 micromol H2O2 uses 8 micromol GSH, forming 4 micromol GSSG.
Each GSSG regenerated needs 1 NADPH, so 4 micromol NADPH are required.
Each glucose-6-phosphate gives 2 NADPH, so 4 / 2 = 2 micromol glucose-6-phosphate.

blocks.answer: 2 micromol of glucose-6-phosphate. In G6PD deficiency this flux cannot be sustained and the oxidant accumulates.

rows: Normal, but not used for the burst
blocks.caption: Two clinical disorders linked to NADPH.

blocks.title: The red cell lifeline
blocks.text: Red cells have no mitochondria, so the pentose phosphate pathway is their only route to NADPH. NADPH keeps glutathione reduced, which protects haemoglobin and the membrane from oxidants. Reduce NADPH and oxidants win.

points: The pentose phosphate pathway has an oxidative phase making 2 NADPH per glucose-6-phosphate and a reversible non-oxidative phase yielding ribose-5-phosphate and glycolytic intermediates.
G6PD is the regulated step, stimulated by NADP+ and inhibited by NADPH.
NADPH drives fatty acid and steroid synthesis, glutathione regeneration, cytochrome P450 reactions and the phagocyte respiratory burst.
G6PD deficiency (X-linked) causes oxidant-triggered haemolysis because red cells have no other NADPH source.

questions.stem: Which are the two principal products of the pentose phosphate pathway?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: NADPH for reductive reactions and ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis.
distractorRationale.b: ATP and pyruvate are products of glycolysis; the PPP makes no net ATP.
distractorRationale.c: NADH and acetyl-CoA arise from pyruvate dehydrogenase and the citric acid cycle.
distractorRationale.d: FADH2 is made in the citric acid cycle and fatty acid oxidation, and glycogen is a storage polymer.

questions.explanation: The oxidative phase generates NADPH and the pathway also yields ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotides and nucleic acids. Neither ATP nor NADH is a product of this pathway.

questions.stem: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting, regulated step of the pentose phosphate pathway, and what stimulates it?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: G6PD is the committed step and is driven by NADP+ and inhibited by NADPH.
distractorRationale.b: Transketolase is a reversible non-oxidative enzyme, not the control point.
distractorRationale.c: Transaldolase is reversible and not regulated by ATP.
distractorRationale.d: 6-Phosphogluconate dehydrogenase is the second oxidative step and is not the main regulated step; NADH is not its regulator.

questions.explanation: G6PD catalyses the first and committed step and responds to the NADP+/NADPH ratio, so the pathway speeds up only when NADPH is being consumed. This matches supply to demand.

questions.stem: Which of the following reactions directly depends on NADPH?

options.text: Regeneration of reduced glutathione by glutathione reductase
Conversion of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase

questions.correctOptionText: Regeneration of reduced glutathione by glutathione reductase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: glutathione reductase uses NADPH to reduce GSSG to 2 GSH.
distractorRationale.b: Lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH, not NADPH.
distractorRationale.c: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reduces NAD+ rather than NADP+.
distractorRationale.d: ATP synthase uses the proton gradient, not NADPH.

questions.explanation: Reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence use NADPH, whereas energy-producing pathways use NADH. Glutathione reductase is the clearest example of NADPH supporting antioxidant protection.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man given primaquine for malaria develops back pain, dark urine and jaundice 3 days later. His blood film shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. Which sequence best explains his haemolysis?

options.text: Oxidant stress, insufficient NADPH, failure to regenerate GSH, oxidised haemoglobin, damaged red cells removed
Excess NADPH, over-reduction of haemoglobin, then red cell swelling
Failure of the Na+/K+-ATPase due to lack of ATP from glycolysis
Excess ribose-5-phosphate causing red cell crenation

questions.correctOptionText: Oxidant stress, insufficient NADPH, failure to regenerate GSH, oxidised haemoglobin, damaged red cells removed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the oxidant drug overwhelms a G6PD-deficient cell that cannot make enough NADPH.
distractorRationale.b: G6PD deficiency causes too little NADPH, not too much.
distractorRationale.c: This describes pyruvate kinase deficiency rather than a drug-triggered oxidant haemolysis with Heinz bodies.
distractorRationale.d: Ribose-5-phosphate is not the problem; the PPP still produces pentoses but NADPH is deficient.

questions.explanation: Primaquine generates oxidants that consume glutathione. Without sufficient NADPH from G6PD, GSH cannot be regenerated, so haemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies and damaged cells are removed by the spleen as bite cells.

questions.stem: Why does G6PD deficiency cause clinical problems mainly in red blood cells rather than in other tissues such as liver?

options.text: Red cells have no mitochondria and no other NADPH source, and cannot synthesise replacement enzyme
G6PD is expressed only in red cells
Red cells use NADPH to make ATP
Liver cells do not use glutathione

questions.correctOptionText: Red cells have no mitochondria and no other NADPH source, and cannot synthesise replacement enzyme

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the pentose phosphate pathway is their only NADPH source and they cannot resynthesise protein.
distractorRationale.b: G6PD is expressed in all cells; the mutation is simply most critical in red cells.
distractorRationale.c: NADPH does not make ATP; it supplies reducing power.
distractorRationale.d: Liver cells use glutathione too, but have alternative NADPH sources and can make new enzyme.

questions.explanation: Other tissues can produce NADPH by additional routes and can replace damaged enzyme by protein synthesis. Red cells, with no nucleus, mitochondria or protein synthesis, have no such back-up, so reduced G6PD activity directly limits their antioxidant defence.

questions.stem: True or false: G6PD deficiency is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait.
questions.explanation: The G6PD gene is on the X chromosome, so males with one mutant allele are affected while heterozygous females are usually carriers with variable expression. This explains why clinically significant haemolysis is more common in males.

questions.stem: A red cell exposed to an oxidant generates 12 micromol of hydrogen peroxide. Glutathione peroxidase uses 2 GSH per H2O2, producing GSSG, and glutathione reductase uses 1 NADPH per GSSG. If all NADPH comes from the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway at 2 NADPH per glucose-6-phosphate, how many micromol of glucose-6-phosphate must be oxidised?
questions.explanation: Each H2O2 yields one GSSG, so 12 micromol H2O2 gives 12 micromol GSSG, which needs 12 micromol NADPH. At 2 NADPH per glucose-6-phosphate this needs 12 / 2 = 6 micromol, a demand that a G6PD-deficient cell cannot meet.

questions.stem: A hepatocyte synthesises 3 molecules of palmitate, each requiring 14 NADPH. If all NADPH were supplied by the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway (2 NADPH per glucose-6-phosphate), how many molecules of glucose-6-phosphate would be oxidised?
questions.explanation: Total NADPH = 3 x 14 = 42. Each glucose-6-phosphate gives 2 NADPH, so 42 / 2 = 21 molecules. This shows how strongly lipogenic tissues depend on the pathway for reducing power.

questions.stem: Describe the oxidative and non-oxidative phases of the pentose phosphate pathway, naming the products of each and what the cell uses them for.
markingGuide: Oxidative phase: G6PD and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase convert glucose-6-phosphate to ribulose-5-phosphate
Oxidative phase produces 2 NADPH and 1 CO2 per glucose-6-phosphate; irreversible
G6PD is rate-limiting, stimulated by NADP+ and inhibited by NADPH
NADPH used for fatty acid and steroid synthesis, glutathione regeneration, cytochrome P450
Non-oxidative phase: reversible transketolase (thiamine pyrophosphate) and transaldolase reactions
Produces ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotides and recycles pentoses to fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
questions.explanation: The oxidative phase is the NADPH source and the non-oxidative phase is the flexible link to nucleotide synthesis and glycolysis. The reversibility of the second phase lets the cell balance its needs for NADPH and ribose.

questions.stem: Explain the importance of NADPH in reductive biosynthesis and in antioxidant defence, giving two examples of each and one clinical disorder that arises when NADPH-dependent function fails.
markingGuide: NADPH is the reductant for biosynthesis; examples: fatty acid synthesis (14 NADPH per palmitate) and cholesterol or steroid synthesis
NADPH is the reductant for antioxidant defence: glutathione reductase regenerates GSH from GSSG, which allows glutathione peroxidase to remove hydrogen peroxide
Other uses: cytochrome P450 and the respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase)
NADPH is separate from NADH, which is used for ATP production
Clinical example: G6PD deficiency causing oxidant-induced haemolysis, with Heinz bodies and bite cells, or chronic granulomatous disease from NADPH oxidase deficiency
questions.explanation: NADPH provides the reducing equivalents that anabolic pathways and glutathione need, and it is distinct from NADH. When it is lacking, as in G6PD deficiency, cells that depend on it for protection against oxidants, particularly red cells, are damaged.
